title: Ricart-Agrawala, step by step
sub: Two processes request the critical section at once; timestamps decide who goes first.

frames.caption: Four processes share one critical section, with no central lock server. Ricart-Agrawala: to enter, a process must get a REPLY from every other process.
P1 and P3 want in at the same time. Each stamps its request with a Lamport timestamp (P1: 3, P3: 5) and sends REQUEST to the other three.
P2 and P4 are not competing, so they REPLY to both at once.

P1 and P3 must judge each other. P3 sees P1's timestamp 3 is earlier than its own 5, so P1 has priority: P3 replies. P1 sees P3's 5 is later than its own 3, so it defers its reply to P3 and holds onto the request.
P1 has all three replies and enters the critical section. P3 has two of three and waits: the missing reply is the one P1 is holding back.

P1 leaves the critical section and sends the deferred REPLY. That reply doubles as the release message, which is why Ricart-Agrawala needs 2(n − 1) messages per entry where Lamport's algorithm needs 3(n − 1).

P3 enters. Two entries, 12 messages: 2 × 2(4 − 1). Ties in timestamp are broken by process id, so every pair of competing requests is ordered the same way at every process, and only one process can hold all the replies at once.
